Sanjeev AI: Frontend Guidelines ​

To maintain a scalable, readable, and highly performant codebase, all React development in this project must adhere to the following guidelines.

1. File Size & Component Splitting ​

  • Maximum File Size: No component file should exceed 300-400 lines of code. If a file exceeds this limit, it is doing too much.
  • Single Responsibility Principle: A component should do one thing well. If a component handles complex state, renders a complex UI, and contains multiple sub-views (e.g., Modals), it must be split.
  • UI vs Logic: Separate complex business logic from UI rendering using Custom Hooks (e.g., useStudioState, useWorkflow).

2. Directory Structure ​

text
src/
  ├── components/      # Reusable UI components (Buttons, Inputs)
  ├── features/        # Feature-specific modules (e.g., /studio, /auth)
  │   └── studio/
  │       ├── hooks/   # Custom hooks (e.g., useDirector.ts)
  │       ├── ui/      # Feature sub-components (e.g., StudioHeader.tsx, AutomationModal.tsx)
  │       └── UnifiedStudio.tsx # The Main Container
  ├── pages/           # Route-level components
  ├── hooks/           # Global hooks (e.g., useAuth)
  └── utils/           # Helper functions

3. Sub-Component Extraction Rules ​

When extracting components from a large monolith (like UnifiedStudio.tsx), follow these steps:

  1. Extract Modals: Popups and modals (e.g., Publish Modal, Automation Modal, Cast Modal) should always be their own files. They usually only rely on a few props (isOpen, onClose, onSubmit).
  2. Extract Independent UI Sections: A header toolbar, a progress stepper, or a sidebar should be isolated into components like <StudioHeader /> and <WorkflowStepper />.
  3. Pass Callbacks, not Setters: Avoid passing setState functions deep into children. Pass semantic callback functions like onLaunchAutomation or onPublish.

4. State Management ​

  • Group related state into custom hooks.
  • Avoid passing more than 4-5 props to a component. If you need more, consider passing a config object or using a context provider.

5. Styling ​

  • Continue using Tailwind CSS.
  • Avoid inline styles unless absolutely necessary (e.g., dynamic width for progress bars).
  • Keep classes readable by extracting long class strings into constants or using clsx/tailwind-merge if conditional logic is complex.

6. Unit Testing & Testability ​

Splitting components is critical for achieving high test coverage and maintainability:

  • Test UI in Isolation: "Dumb" UI components (e.g., WorkflowStepper.tsx) can be tested purely with mock props (e.g., passing a fake workflowState object) without needing to mock Firebase, Auth, or complex contexts.
  • Test Logic in Isolation: Custom Hooks (e.g., useAutomation.ts) can be tested independently of the UI using libraries like @testing-library/react-hooks.
  • Mocking: The smaller the component, the less mocking is required. Monolithic components often require incredibly complex test setups that break easily.
  • Test File Conventions: Name your unit tests *.test.ts/tsx and your Playwright tests *.spec.ts/tsx. These are strictly excluded in tsconfig.app.json from the production build to ensure testing libraries (like vi) do not contaminate or break the main application build step.

Testing Environment Strategy ​

IMPORTANT

CRITICAL RULE FOR AI AGENTS:

  1. Local Testing: When running or writing tests locally (both E2E Playwright tests and Vitest Unit/Integration tests), they MUST run against the Local Firebase Emulators.
  2. GitHub CI Testing: When tests run in GitHub Actions (after a push), they will run against the live sanjeev-ai-staging or sanjeev-ai Firebase projects using Custom Tokens. Do NOT configure local tests to hit live Firebase databases.

7. In-File Documentation (Self-Contained Context) ​

To ensure independent future feature analysis is easy, all code files must contain a self-contained documentation block at the top of the file. This block must include:

  1. Description: What this file does.
  2. Parent Component(s): Where this component/hook is used (e.g., consumed by UnifiedStudio.tsx).
  3. Dependencies / Children: What other services or sub-components this file relies on (e.g., depends on Firebase Firestore, renders VideoScrubber).

Example:

tsx
/**
 * @file StudioToolbar.tsx
 * @description Renders the top-right action buttons in the Unified Studio (Automate, Director, Audio, Export).
 * 
 * @parent UnifiedStudio.tsx (Main Container)
 * @dependencies React, SanjeevAI Icon Components
 */

8. UX Guidelines for Mobile and Desktop ​

To ensure consistency and robustness across our interfaces, follow these UX/UI patterns:

Responsive Header Layouts ​

Complex headers (Title + Tabs + Actions) must not break or overflow on small screens. Use CSS Flexbox ordering to control responsive wrapping:

  • Top Row (Mobile): Keep the Title (order-1) and Action Buttons (e.g., ⋮, X) (order-2, ml-auto) on the top line.
  • Second Row (Mobile): Push Tabs (order-3, w-full) to wrap onto their own full-width line below the title.
  • Desktop: The same markup can gracefully reflow into a single line (w-auto for tabs, order-2 for tabs, order-3 for actions) simply by toggling breakpoints (e.g., sm:order-2).

Preventing "Button Crowding" ​

  • Truncation: Always allow titles and large text blocks to shrink (min-w-0, shrink) and truncate with ellipses rather than pushing interactive elements off-screen.
  • Dropdown Menus: If action buttons (Automate, Export, Import, etc.) fight for horizontal space, wrap them into a "More Options" (⋮ or MoreVertical) dropdown menu. Trigger this collapse early (e.g., at the xl breakpoint or permanently) rather than relying on horizontal scrolling for critical actions.

Consistency in "Create New" Actions ​

  • Persistent Access: When managing lists of assets (Scripts, Characters, Locations), users must always be able to append a new item without relying solely on an empty-state screen or a hidden menu.
  • Pattern: Include a prominent + Add Line button at the bottom of the script list, or a large dashed ➕ Add [Item] card at the very end of asset grids.
  • Empty States: Empty states should also explicitly offer a primary button to create the very first asset from scratch.

Layout Stability ​

  • Avoid absolute positioning for major layout toggles (like Tab Switchers). Place them in the normal document flow (e.g., as a dedicated block or flex column) to prevent z-index wars, overlapping, or cut-offs with scrolling containers.
